tips.title: OR and XOR differ in one row only
tips.body: They agree on three rows of four and disagree when **both inputs are 1**: OR gives **1**, XOR gives **0**. Check that row first and you can identify either gate in seconds.

tips.title: Count up in binary
tips.body: 00, 01, 10, 11 for two inputs; 000 through 111 for three. Listing them any other way risks a missed or repeated row; counting up makes every combination appear exactly once.

tips.title: Work in columns, not rows
tips.body: Add a working column for each bracket, then combine them. One simple rule applied eight times beats reading the whole expression eight times — and a slip in the final column can be found by checking the working columns.

tips.title: Plus means OR, so 1 + 1 = 1
tips.body: Boolean notation borrows arithmetic symbols but not arithmetic. **+** is OR, **.** is AND, **⊕** is XOR, an **overbar** is NOT. Read `1 + 1` as *1 OR 1*, and it is 1.

tips.title: NAND and NOR are not on your course
tips.body: The specification says so in as many words. If a textbook or a video covers them, that is time you could spend on three-input truth tables, which are examined.

why.matters:
Underneath every program there is no arithmetic and no text — only wires that are on or off, and gates that decide what an on or an off leads to. Boolean logic is that layer written down.

It is worth learning for two quite separate reasons. It is how the hardware actually works, so it explains what a processor is made of. And it is the same logic as the conditions in an `IF`, so getting `AND` and `OR` exactly right on paper is the same skill as getting a condition right in code — where being nearly right lets every wrong case through.

examples.title: Why a microwave will not start with the door open
examples.body:
Two things have to be true at once: the door is shut **and** the start button is pressed. Either one on its own does nothing. That is an `AND` gate, and it is wired into the machine rather than written in software, because a safety rule you can reprogram is not a safety rule.

The truth table is the whole specification of the behaviour: four rows, one output that is 1, and no argument possible about the other three. That is why a table is a better answer than a description — a table cannot be vague.

props.label: D = door shut, S = start pressed

visual.alt: An AND gate with two inputs, the door being shut and the start button being pressed, and its truth table showing the output is 1 on only one of the four rows, when both inputs are 1

examples.title: Why OR and XOR only disagree once
examples.body:
"Tea or coffee?" means one of them. `OR` in logic means **at least** one, including both — and that single difference is the one to learn.

The two gates agree on three of their four rows. They part company only when both inputs are 1: `OR` gives 1, `XOR` gives 0. Most of what makes XOR tricky is that one row, so if you check it first you can tell which gate a table describes without reading the rest.

visual.alt: A truth table with OR and XOR side by side for two inputs: the two columns match on the first three rows and differ only on the last, where both inputs are 1 and OR gives 1 while XOR gives 0

examples.title: Why three inputs mean eight rows and not six
examples.body:
Each input can be 0 or 1, so adding an input **doubles** the number of combinations: 2 rows for one input, 4 for two, 8 for three, 16 for four. Two to the power of the inputs, every time.

Knowing the count before you start is how you avoid an easy mistake: a table with a row missing. Write them out counting up in binary — 000, 001, 010 — and the order does the remembering for you, because every combination appears exactly once.

visual.alt: A table of how many rows a truth table needs: two rows for one input, four for two, eight for three and sixteen for four, doubling each time because each input can be 0 or 1

steps.title: Four gates, and only four
steps.body:
A **logic gate** takes one or two inputs, each of which is **0 or 1**, and produces a single output that is also 0 or 1. Everything a processor does is built from them.

The specification names **four**, and is unusually explicit that these are all you need:

- **NOT** — one input. The output is the **opposite** of the input.
- **AND** — the output is 1 **only if both** inputs are 1.
- **OR** — the output is 1 **if either or both** inputs are 1.
- **XOR** — *exclusive OR*. The output is 1 **if exactly one** input is 1, but **not both**.

**Students do not need to know about or use NAND and NOR logic gates.**

That is the specification's own sentence. If you meet NAND or NOR in a textbook, it is not on your course.

The one that needs care is **XOR**, because it differs from OR in exactly **one row**: when **both** inputs are 1, **OR gives 1** but **XOR gives 0**. Everything else about them is identical, and that single row is the one to check first.

steps.title: Building a truth table
steps.body:
A **truth table** lists **every possible combination** of the inputs and the output for each. Building one is mechanical, and doing it in a fixed order is what stops rows being missed.

**How many rows?** Two inputs give $2^2 = 4$ rows; three inputs give $2^3 = 8$. The specification takes you up to **three inputs**, so eight rows is the largest table you will need.

**In what order?** Count up in **binary**. For two inputs: 00, 01, 10, 11. For three: 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111. Any order gives a correct table if every row is there, but counting up in binary makes a missing or repeated row easy to spot.

Row 00: neither is 1, so the output is **0**
Row 01 and row 10: exactly one is 1, so **1** each
Row 11: **both** are 1, so the output is **0** — this is where XOR differs from OR

steps.title: Writing Boolean expressions
steps.body:
As well as gates and tables, the specification asks you to write and read **Boolean expressions**, using a specific notation. Learn the symbols exactly, because they are not the ones used in programming:

- **.** represents the **AND** gate
- **+** represents the **OR** gate
- **⊕** represents the **XOR** gate
- an **overbar** represents the **NOT** gate

So the expression for *(A AND B) OR (NOT C)* is written:

$$A . B + \overline{C}$$

Two things about the notation catch people out.

**The symbols look like arithmetic but are not.** `+` here means **OR**, not addition — so `1 + 1 = 1` in Boolean algebra, because *1 OR 1* is 1. And `.` means AND, not multiply, though the analogy happens to work for AND.

**The overbar covers what it applies to.** $\overline{C}$ is NOT C. $\overline{A . B}$ would be NOT (A AND B) — the bar stretching across both letters means the whole expression is inverted. Where you end the bar changes the meaning.

**Brackets** work as they do in arithmetic: they say what to do first.

steps.title: A table with three inputs
steps.body:
Three inputs mean **eight rows**, and the way to keep it right is to work in **columns, not rows**: build a column for each part of the expression, then combine them.

Doing it row by row means re-reading the whole expression eight times. Doing it by column means applying one simple rule eight times, which is far harder to get wrong.

visuals.problem: Complete the truth table for Q = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)

steps.text: List A, B, C counting up in binary: 000 through 111
Add a **working column** for **A AND B**: 1 only in the rows where both are 1
Add another for **NOT C**: the opposite of the C column
**Q** is those two columns **ORed**: 1 wherever **either** working column is 1
Q reads **1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1** down the eight rows
Check the last row: A=1, B=1, C=1 gives (1 AND 1) OR (NOT 1) = 1 OR 0 = **1** ✓

steps.title: Reading a table the other way
steps.body:
Questions do not only ask you to **build** a table — they ask you to **interpret** one. That means answering questions like *for which inputs is the output 1?* or *which gate does this table describe?*

**Identifying a gate from its table** is the one to practise first. With two inputs there are only four outputs to compare, and the four you know are:

- **0, 0, 0, 1** → **AND** (only the last row)
- **0, 1, 1, 1** → **OR** (all but the first)
- **0, 1, 1, 0** → **XOR** (the middle two)
- **1, 0** → **NOT** (one input only)

The pair to look at carefully is **OR and XOR**: they agree on the first three rows and differ only on the **last**, where both inputs are 1. So when identifying a gate, **look at the bottom row first** — it settles OR against XOR immediately, and nothing else does.

**Interpreting in context.** A question may describe a system — an alarm that sounds when a door is open **and** the system is armed — and ask which gate it is. Translate the English into the rule: *only when both* is **AND**; *either or both* is **OR**; *one but not both* is **XOR**; *the opposite of* is **NOT**.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the four logic gates on the specification, and say how many inputs each takes.
2. How many rows does a truth table with three inputs have?
3. Write the Boolean symbols for AND, OR, XOR and NOT.

**Part B.**

4. Build the truth table for an OR gate, and for an XOR gate. In which row do they differ?
5. Build the truth table for Q = A . B (that is, A AND B).
6. A gate's output column reads 0, 1, 1, 0. Which gate is it?

**Part C.**

7. Build the eight-row truth table for Q = (A OR B) AND (NOT C).
8. A door alarm sounds when the door is open **and** the alarm is armed. Which gate is this, and what would the table look like?

For question 7, add a working column for each bracket before filling in Q. Eight rows done row-by-row is where mistakes come from.

steps.title: Going deeper: the row that separates OR from XOR
steps.body:
**If you remember one thing.** OR and XOR agree on three of their four rows. They differ **only** when **both inputs are 1**: OR gives **1**, XOR gives **0**. That row is the one to check, and checking it first identifies a gate faster than working through the whole table.

The name says it: **exclusive** OR — *one or the other, but not both*. Everyday English often means XOR when it says *or*: *you can have tea or coffee* usually excludes having both. The logical OR does **not** exclude it, which is why the two need different gates at all.

**Why work in columns.** An eight-row table done row by row means reading and evaluating the whole expression eight separate times — eight chances to slip. Done in columns, you apply one simple rule eight times, then another, then combine. The working columns also make a slip **easy to find**: if the final column has an error, the working shows where it came from, and a bare answer shows nothing.

**Boolean algebra is not arithmetic.** `+` is OR, so `1 + 1 = 1`, which looks wrong until you read it as *1 OR 1 is 1*. `.` is AND, and there the arithmetic analogy happens to hold: `1 . 1 = 1` and `1 . 0 = 0`, exactly like multiplication. That coincidence is why AND is sometimes called the *product* and OR the *sum* — but only AND actually behaves like its arithmetic namesake.

**The overbar's reach matters.** $\overline{A} . B$ means *(NOT A) AND B*. $\overline{A . B}$ means *NOT (A AND B)*. They are different functions — check the row where A=1 and B=1: the first gives 0 (because NOT A is 0), and the second gives 0 as well; but at A=0, B=0 the first gives 0 and the second gives 1. When you read an expression, look at **how far the bar extends** before doing anything else.

**And one thing not to revise.** The specification states that NAND and NOR are **not** required. Time spent on them is time not spent on the three-input tables that are.

visuals.alt: The truth table for an XOR gate placed for comparison, showing zero in the final row where OR would give one

props.title: One row in four is the whole difference

visuals.alt: A table comparing OR and XOR row by row, showing they differ only in the last

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The four gates on the specification are **NOT, AND, OR and XOR**. **NAND and NOR are not required.**
- **NOT** flips its single input. **AND** gives 1 only when **both** inputs are 1.
- **OR** gives 1 when **either or both** inputs are 1. **XOR** gives 1 when **exactly one** is.
- **OR and XOR differ only in the last row**, where both inputs are 1: OR gives 1, XOR gives 0.
- A truth table lists **every combination** of the inputs: $2^n$ rows for $n$ inputs.
- Two inputs give **4** rows, three give **8** — and three is the most the specification asks for.
- List the inputs by **counting up in binary**, so no row is missed or repeated.
- Boolean notation: **.** is AND, **+** is OR, **⊕** is XOR, an **overbar** is NOT.
- `+` means OR, so **1 + 1 = 1**. It is not addition.
- The **reach of the overbar** changes the meaning: $\overline{A} . B$ is not $\overline{A . B}$.
- Build a three-input table in **columns**: one per bracket, then combine. The working columns make slips easy to find.
- Identify a gate from its output column, and check the **bottom row** first to settle OR against XOR.

questions.prompt: Construct the truth table for Q = (A AND B) OR (NOT C), showing your working columns, and state for how many of the eight rows the output is 1.
questions.solution: There are three inputs, so the table needs two to the power of three, which is eight rows. The inputs A, B and C are listed counting up in binary, from zero zero zero to one one one. A working column is then added for A AND B, which contains a one only in the two rows where both A and B are one, that is the last two rows. A second working column is added for NOT C, which contains the opposite of the C column, so it is one in every row where C is zero, which is every other row starting from the first. The output column Q is obtained by taking the OR of the two working columns, so Q is one wherever either working column contains a one. Reading down the eight rows, Q is one, zero, one, zero, one, zero, one, one. Counting these, the output is one in five of the eight rows. As a check, the final row has A equals one, B equals one and C equals one, which gives one AND one, that is one, OR NOT one, that is zero, and one OR zero is one, which matches the table.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The size.** Three inputs, so $2^3 = \mathbf{8}$ rows.

**The order.** List A, B, C **counting up in binary**: 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111.

**Working column 1 — A AND B.** A 1 only where **both** A and B are 1: the last two rows.

**Working column 2 — NOT C.** The **opposite** of the C column: 1 wherever C is 0, so every other row starting from the first.

**The output.** Q is the two working columns **ORed** — 1 wherever **either** is 1:

$$Q = 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 1$$

The output is 1 in **five** of the eight rows.

**Check one row in full.** The last: A=1, B=1, C=1 gives $(1 \text{ AND } 1) \text{ OR } (\text{NOT } 1) = 1 \text{ OR } 0 = 1$ ✓

Show the **working columns**. If the final column slips, the working shows where; a bare answer shows nothing.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an OR gate and an XOR gate, and explain why the distinction matters when translating an everyday description into a logic gate.
questions.solution: An OR gate gives an output of one when either of its inputs is one, and also when both of them are one. An XOR gate, which stands for exclusive OR, gives an output of one when exactly one of its inputs is one, but gives zero when both of them are one. This means that the two gates produce identical outputs for three of the four rows of their truth tables, and differ only in the final row, where both inputs are one: there the OR gate gives one and the XOR gate gives zero. The distinction matters when translating everyday descriptions because the word or in ordinary English very often means exclusive or. If a menu says that a meal comes with soup or a salad, it is usually understood that the customer may have one of them but not both, and that is an XOR. By contrast, if a system is described as sounding an alarm when the front door is open or the back door is open, the alarm should certainly sound when both are open, and that is an ordinary OR. Reading the description carefully to decide whether both together should give an output of one is therefore essential before choosing the gate.

questions.modelAnswer:
**OR** gives 1 when **either** input is 1 — **and also when both are**.

**XOR** — *exclusive OR* — gives 1 when **exactly one** input is 1, and **0 when both are**.

**The difference.** Their truth tables are **identical for three of the four rows**. They differ only in the last, where **both inputs are 1**: OR gives **1**, XOR gives **0**.

**Why it matters in translation.** Everyday English very often means **exclusive** or:

- *The meal comes with soup or salad* — normally one **but not both**: **XOR**.
- *The alarm sounds when the front door or the back door is open* — it should certainly sound when **both** are open: **OR**.

**How to decide.** Ask one question of the description: **should both together give an output of 1?** If yes, it is OR; if no, it is XOR. That single test settles every case, and it is exactly the row the two gates disagree on.

questions.prompt: Give the output column of the truth table for Q = A ⊕ (B . C), with the rows in the order ABC = 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111, as eight digits with no spaces.
questions.solution: Work in columns. **B . C** is 1 only where B and C are both 1: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1. **A** is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1. XOR gives 1 where exactly one of those two columns is 1: **00011110**. Check the last row: A = 1 and B . C = 1, so 1 ⊕ 1 = 0.

questions.prompt: Which is (A OR B) AND (NOT C), written in the specification's notation?
questions.solution: OR is **+**, AND is **.** and NOT is an **overbar** over C alone: $(A + B) . \overline{C}$. Swapping the dot and the plus gives (A AND B) OR (NOT C), a bar over everything would invert the whole expression, and ⊕ is XOR.

markScheme.description: (A + B) . C with a bar over C only

examTechnique.body:
Work out how many rows the table needs before drawing it: two to the power of the number of inputs.

List the input combinations by counting up in binary, so none is missed.

Add a working column for each bracketed part of the expression, then combine them for the output. The working columns show where any slip came from.

When identifying a gate from a table, check the row where both inputs are 1 first: it separates OR from XOR immediately.

Use the specification's symbols: a dot for AND, a plus for OR, a circled plus for XOR, and an overbar for NOT.

Check one row by working the whole expression through in full before moving on.
examinerErrors: Giving XOR the same output as OR when both inputs are 1.
Missing a row, usually by not listing the inputs in binary order.
Reading + as addition, so writing 1 + 1 = 2 or 10.
Confusing the dot for AND with multiplication in a way that changes the answer.
Ignoring how far the overbar extends.
Revising NAND and NOR, which the specification excludes.
Filling in a three-input table row by row and slipping on one row.
Giving only the output column with no working when working was asked for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer knows that OR and XOR differ in exactly one row and uses that to identify gates rather than working through whole tables. It builds three-input tables in **columns**, so a slip costs one cell rather than a row, and it shows those columns so any slip can be traced. It reads Boolean notation precisely, including how far an overbar reaches. And translating an everyday description, it asks the one question that settles it — should both together give 1? — instead of guessing between OR and XOR.
